Several linguistic features were correlated with symptom severity and language performance. Linguistic disturbances in patients with SZ were heterogeneous and more pronounced in Cog-D group compared to Cog-ND group. These findings highlight the potential of NLP-based speech analysis for identifying cognitive impairment and support the cross-linguistic generalizability of linguistic markers.

title: Exploratory genetic and expression analysis identifies MCTP2 associated with negative symptom improvement in schizophrenia
abstract: Abstract Negative symptoms are common initial manifestations of schizophrenia, and their improvement is key to social function prognosis. MCTP2, a C2 domain-containing protein, is involved in higher cognitive functions and critical for facial recognition. We hypothesized MCTP2 may be associated with negative symptom improvement in schizophrenia patients receiving antipsychotics. A genome-wide association study was performed in Han Chinese schizophrenia patients to explore the association between genetic polymorphisms and antipsychotic response, focusing on PANSS negative (PANSS-N) symptom reduction after 6-week aripiprazole or ziprasidone monotherapy. The eQTL gene expression, protein–protein interaction network, and network pharmacology analyses were conducted to clarify the regulatory mechanism and molecular networks. An association was identified between MCTP2 polymorphism rs28502452 ( P = 8.01×10⁻⁶) and PANSS-N symptom reduction. Patients with alleles linked to higher MCTP2 expression had greater PANSS-N reduction. Expression analyses in schizophrenia, Alzheimer’s disease and autism confirmed MCTP2’s positive regulation of normal cognitive functions. Protein–protein interaction analysis revealed a calcium signaling cluster (SLITRK5, NCALD, CPNE5), and the calcium signaling pathway is major in the network pharmacology of aripiprazole and ziprasidone. Furthermore, synaptic proteins SLITRK5 and PTPRD may regulate the interaction network between MCTP2 and BTBD9, the latter two of which are high-risk genes for improving negative symptoms. This study demonstrates MCTP2’s involvement in schizophrenia negative symptoms, confirms its positive role in cognitive function, and identifies the synaptic calcium signaling network. These findings provide a foundation for future research on negative symptoms, cognitive impairment, and targeted therapies.

title: Genetic risk of psychopathology predicts environmental risk
abstract: Abstract Environmental risk factors for psychosis and psychopathology are often treated as non-genetic, although many are partly heritable or correlated with genetically influenced traits. We tested nine polygenic scores against 49 environmental-risk factors in 307,493 UK Biobank participants without recorded schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or major depressive disorder diagnoses or antipsychotic medication use. Polygenic scores were generated using PRS-CS and tested in 441 standardised linear models with HC1 robust standard errors. Across all models, 212 associations survived within-score false-discovery-rate correction. ADHD, educational attainment, major depression, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder polygenic scores showed the broadest profiles, but associations differed across five environmental-risk categories. In a secondary analysis excluding victimisation and behavioural measures, seven perception/subjectivity factors showed stronger pooled associations than 25 objective/non-perception factors for schizophrenia, major depression, ADHD, bipolar disorder and neuroticism polygenic scores. Four conceptually tighter matched comparisons produced a similar but non-uniform pattern. Effects were small and do not establish causality. Measured environmental risk is partly correlated with inherited liability through behavioural, social, socioeconomic, cognitive, and perception-related pathways.

title: Predictors of remission in individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Individuals at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis (CHR-P) show highly variable outcomes, with approximately one-third achieving remission from their CHR-P state at follow-up. Understanding which factors are associated with remission is crucial for refining risk stratification and optimising early interventions in this group. Following a pre-registered protocol (CRD42024512653), a PRISMA-compliant systematic review was conducted. A multistep literature search was conducted across five databases, to identify studies reporting factors associated with remission among individuals at CHR-P. Four independent reviewers extracted data on sociodemographic, clinical, functioning, neurocognitive, electrophysiological, peripheral neurochemical and genetic markers, psychosocial/environmental, and linguistic factors. Risk of bias was assessed using a modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS). Owing to substantial heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was performed. Fifty-one longitudinal studies ( n = 10,073; mean age 19.1 years (study-level range 13.8–28.4); 47.7% females from 15 countries were included, with follow-up ranging from 8 to 72 months. Most studies were of high methodological quality (NOS mean = 7.7; 92.1% rated high quality). Replicated predictors of remission were: higher baseline functioning ( n = 10), lower baseline levels of attenuated positive symptom severity ( n = 7), lower negative symptoms ( n = 3), and lower self-disturbance ( n = 2)-, – higher baseline verbal learning ( n = 4), verbal, working and visual ( n = 2 each)-, preserved MMN amplitude ( n = 3)-, and speech fluency and connectedness ( n = 2). Findings suggest that remission in CHR-P is consistently associated with lower symptom severity at baseline, preserved functioning, and better cognitive performance, while emerging evidence also highlights the potential role of self-disturbance, linguistic features and electrophysiological markers. However, substantial heterogeneity across studies limits direct comparability, and potentially protective factors associated with favourable outcomes remain underexplored. Future translation into clinical practice will require integration of information across domains rather than relying on single-domain indicators.

title: Neural correlates of peripheral inflammation in individuals with first-episode schizophrenia
abstract: Abstract Elevated pro-inflammatory markers have been reported in schizophrenia, and inflammation has been found to modulate brain functional connectivity. This paper provides novel evidence on the association between striatal connectivity and inflammation in first-episode schizophrenia (FES) and its relationship with negative symptoms and cognitive performance. We included 132 individuals with FES who underwent resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) as part of the Benefit of Minocycline on negative symptoms of schizophrenia (BeneMin) trial. We applied a previously estimated semi-supervised machine learning clustering solution on inflammatory patterns to assign individuals with FES to an inflammation group at baseline and at 12-month follow-up. A seed-based functional connectivity analysis was conducted using bilateral basal ganglia as seed regions. Symptoms of psychosis were evaluated using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). The Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) was used as a proxy for cognitive function. At baseline, FES individuals in the elevated CRP group (High-CRP) presented higher functional connectivity between the right nucleus accumbens and the left middle frontal gyrus and between the right pallidum and the left middle frontal gyrus/precentral gyrus, compared with individuals in the low inflammation group (Low-Inf). These differences were also evident at follow-up, although they did not reach statistical significance. We found a greater correlation between right nucleus accumbens—left superior and middle frontal gyri functional connectivity and PANSS negative symptom subscale scores in the High-CRP group compared with the Low-Inf group. Our findings suggest that inflammation is associated with differences in fronto-striatal connectivity early in schizophrenia, which could, in turn, be associated with more severe negative symptoms. Greater fronto-striatal connectivity may represent a distinct neural signature associated with greater inflammation. Interventions aiming at reducing inflammation may represent novel strategies for modulating striatal connectivity and ameliorating negative symptoms.

title: Diagnostic heterogeneity and clozapine use among patients referred for suspected treatment-resistant schizophrenia
abstract: Patients referred for suspected treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) may constitute a diagnostically heterogeneous population. We retrospectively studied 392 patients referred to an outpatient service for suspected TRS. Electronic clinical records were reviewed, and patients classified according to ICD-10 after specialist reassessment. Treatment patterns and factors associated with clozapine exposure were examined across diagnostic groups. A substantial proportion of patients were classified outside schizophrenia (F20), particularly as organic psychotic disorders (F06) or unspecified psychosis (F29). Patients with schizophrenia (F20) and schizoaffective disorder (F25) showed higher clozapine exposure and greater antipsychotic burden, whereas F06 and F29 groups showed lower pharmacological intensification. F29 diagnosis was independently associated with lower odds of clozapine exposure compared with F20. Patients referred for suspected TRS are diagnostically and therapeutically heterogeneous. Diagnostic reassessment is important, and clozapine exposure should be interpreted within the diagnostic and treatment context rather than as a stand-alone marker of TRS status.

title: Lipid profiles and treatment response across symptom-based subgroups in acute schizophrenia: a post-hoc analysis of a randomized clinical trial
abstract: Clinical heterogeneity in schizophrenia complicates treatment optimization and contributes to substantial variability in antipsychotic response. Symptom-based stratification may help to identify more homogeneous patient groups and improve prediction of treatment outcomes. However, evidence from large longitudinal studies remain limited. Metabolic abnormalities are also highly prevalent in schizophrenia and may contribute to differential treatment response across clinical subgroups. We conducted a post hoc analysis of a multicenter randomized clinical trial including 2,990 patients with acute schizophrenia. Symptom-based subgroups were identified using K-means clustering. Baseline metabolic indices were compared across subgroups, and 6-week treatment outcomes were evaluated using logistic regression and mixed-effects models for longitudinal symptom trajectories. Mediation analyses were performed to assess whether metabolic markers contributed to subgroup-related differences in treatment response. There are three subgroups were identified: a negative symptom-predominant subgroup (N, n = 1,010), a positive symptom-predominant subgroup with lower overall severity (P, n = 1,226), and a globally severe subgroup (S, n = 754). Treatment response and symptom-improvement trajectories differed significantly across subgroups. Baseline triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels were higher in Cluster N, whereas high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels were higher in Cluster S. Mediation analyses further showed that LDL-C significantly mediated subgroup differences in treatment response. Overall, our study suggested that symptom-based subgroups in acute schizophrenia showed differences in metabolic profiles and antipsychotic treatment responses. LDL-C may partially account for subgroup-related variability in short-term clinical outcomes, highlighting a potential link between metabolic status and treatment heterogeneity in schizophrenia.

title: Automated speech analysis for psychosis detection: a systematic comparison of task efficiency and feature groups
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the effectiveness of automatic speech analysis in differentiating between patients with psychotic disorders and healthy control individuals with low or high levels of schizotypy within a German-speaking cohort. A range of acoustic and linguistic features was extracted from audio recordings and transcriptions obtained through structured interviews, open discourse, and picture description tasks, in which each participant described at least six pictures. These features served as input to train Random Forest classifiers, with linguistic features achieving consistent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of around 0.8–0.9 across all interview formats. In contrast, acoustic features performed significantly worse, particularly in the picture description task. Using linguistic features, we showed that increasing the number of described pictures significantly improved model accuracy, with performance plateauing after the combination of three pictures. Subsequent feature importance analysis revealed that patients produced simpler language, shorter sentences, less speech overall, and exhibited lower semantic coherence compared to healthy controls. These findings highlight the potential of automatic linguistic analysis as a scalable and objective tool for the detection of psychotic disorders in German-speaking populations.

title: Schizophrenia research in 2026: report from the annual meeting of the Schizophrenia International Research Society
abstract: Abstract SIRS 2026, held under the theme “Schizophrenia Research in the Era of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together researchers, clinicians, and persons with lived experience to take stock of a field whose tools for measuring, predicting, and intervening in psychosis have expanded rapidly. Themes spanned artificial intelligence, automated speech analysis, retinal imaging, computational modelling, and novel psychosocial and pharmacological targets, with evidence that, individually, warrants cautious but serious attention and that, collectively, points toward a more mechanistically grounded psychiatry. A recurring call across the meeting was for rigorous external validation, equitable implementation, and sustained scrutiny of underlying assumptions, including whether existing diagnostic categories and treatment targets remain adequate. Some areas remained underworked relative to their importance, including translating basic neuroscience advances into questions relevant to patients and families, and the structural determinants of illness onset and treatment access. Perhaps the most significant development at SIRS 2026 was not any single scientific finding but the broadening of whose voices and experiences are treated as evidence worth taking seriously in this era of AI, a shift whose consolidation remains a question for the field as much as for any individual programme of work.

title: Probing severe cognitive impairment in treatment resistant schizophrenia: a proof-of-concept in vivo study with (18F)-Flutemetamol PET
abstract: Abstract Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) affects almost 30% of patients with the disorder. This condition is associated with functional impairment and has been suggested to have a putatively different neurobiology compared to non-treatment-resistant schizophrenia. One striking feature of TRS is the presence of relevant cognitive deficits, which, in many cases, align with a Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI)‑like clinical profile without implying amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology. Conversely, aspects of MCI partially overlap with the trajectory of schizophrenia, motivating investigation of putative common factors of convergence. Despite its relevance, in vivo data directly addressing this question are lacking. We used ¹⁸(F)-Flutemetamol Positron Emission Tomography (PET) to investigate regional cortical Aβ deposition and its potential association with clinical symptoms in patients with TRS with MCI‑like cognitive impairment (TRS-MCI). TRS-MCI ( n = 12) underwent a PET scan and clinical evaluation, including the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) and the Brief Assessment of Cognition in Schizophrenia (BACS). PET image analysis was performed using the Diagnosis ORIented ANalysis software, which provides different semiquantitative indices of regional cortical Aβ PET measures. PET data obtained in TRS-MCI were compared with those of amyloid-negative cognitively impaired patients (Aβ- CI) without psychiatric disorders ( n = 12). Group‑level comparisons using expert visual assessment and semi‑automated quantification showed no significant differences. Exploratory correlation within TRS‑MCI revealed a negative association between the regional Aβ composite scores in the Right Parietal Cortex and the PANSS Positive score ( P ≤ 0.01). This pilot study found no evidence of increased cortical Aβ deposition in TRS patients; nevertheless, regional variation in Parietal Cortex ( 18 F)‑Flutemetamol PET signal within the Aβ‑negative range was associated with positive symptoms, warranting confirmation in larger, longitudinal cohorts.

title: From bias to signal: the prognostic meaning of baseline pharmacotherapy in clinical high-risk for psychosis
abstract: Observational evidence is increasingly central to prognostic precision in early intervention in mental health, particularly in Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis (CHR-P) populations where trajectories are heterogeneous and clinical decisions unfold sequentially. In this context, baseline pharmacological exposure should not be treated merely as a nuisance variable or dismissed because it may reflect confounding by indication, confounding by severity, or protopathic bias. These mechanisms limit causal interpretation, but they may also explain why treatment exposure carries prognostic information. Antipsychotic, antidepressant, benzodiazepine, or combined exposure at CHR-P inception may encode prior clinical deterioration, symptom burden, comorbidity, treatment-seeking pathways, clinician concern, partial treatment response, or pharmacologically attenuated expression of emerging psychosis. Current prognostic models often prioritize demographic, symptomatic, cognitive, and functional predictors while giving insufficient attention to baseline pharmacotherapy, despite its availability, clinical interpretability, and temporal relevance. Incorporating medication exposure, dose, duration, indication, adherence, severity, and longitudinal treatment changes may improve risk stratification, reduce hidden heterogeneity, and support more precise evaluation of preventive interventions. The key implication is methodological and clinical: treatment exposure should be interpreted with causal humility but prognostic pragmatism. In CHR-P research, medication history is not simply a source of bias; it is part of the longitudinal clinical record and may help identify prognostically non-equivalent subgroups.

title: Pretreatment plasma amino acid profiles in first-episode schizophrenia: a case-control study with exploratory clinical correlates
abstract: Amino acid dysregulation has been implicated in schizophrenia, but baseline plasma amino acid profiles in first-episode schizophrenia and their clinical relevance remain unclear. We hypothesized that antipsychotic-naïve patients would show distinct amino acid alterations associated with subsequent clinical improvement. Plasma levels of 31 amino acids were measured by ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry in 80 antipsychotic-naïve patients with first-episode schizophrenia and 40 healthy controls. Between-group differences were assessed using Mann–Whitney U tests with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Amino acid-derived indices, receiver operating characteristic analysis, and Spearman correlation analyses were used to characterize metabolic patterns, discriminatory performance, and associations with PANSS improvement. Discriminatory performance was further evaluated using repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with feature selection performed independently within each training set, and multiple testing in the exploratory clinical correlation analyses was controlled using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Eleven amino acids differed significantly between patients and controls after false discovery rate correction. Patients showed lower kynurenine, arginine, homoarginine, aminoadipic acid, and methionine, and higher ornithine, alanine, glutamate, serine, glycine, and GABA. Arginine/ornithine, kynurenine/tryptophan, citrulline/arginine, and tyrosine/phenylalanine ratios also differed between groups. A multivariable amino acid model showed an apparent AUC of 0.949, while repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation yielded a mean out-of-fold AUC of 0.869 (SD = 0.011). In exploratory analyses among patients with paired PANSS data ( n = 26), the baseline glutamate/GABA ratio was negatively associated with improvement in PANSS positive symptoms and remained significant after false discovery rate correction (ρ = −0.618, q = 0.015). However, this association was attenuated and no longer significant after additional adjustment for baseline PANSS positive score. Antipsychotic-naïve first-episode schizophrenia was associated with plasma amino acid abnormalities involving arginine-related metabolism, kynurenine pathway activity, aromatic amino acid conversion, and glutamate/GABA-related balance. These findings support the relevance of peripheral amino acid metabolism in first-episode schizophrenia but require validation in independent cohorts.

Ordinal reduction of frontotemporal sulcal asymmetry with increasing auditory verbal hallucinations in schizophrenia spectrum disorders
abstract: Abstract Asymmetry in paracingulate sulcus (PCS) length and superior temporal sulcus (STS) depth was examined in schizophrenia spectrum patients stratified by auditory verbal hallucination (AVH) frequency. An ordinal reduction in sulcal asymmetry was observed with increasing AVH frequency, reaching statistical significance only for STS depth. The decline in effect size from frequent to less frequent AVH may explain prior inconsistent findings from binary AVH classifications that disregard clinical heterogeneity.
